------------------------------------------
One of the prominent teachers of the Viśiṣṭādvaita philosophy and the श्रीवैष्णव sect, मणवाऌअ मामुनि was born in A.

at Tirukkuruhūr of Tamil Nadu. His parents were Tātaraṇṇar Araiyar and Śrīraṅga Nācciyār.
He was educated first by his ड़थेर् and later by two well-known teachers of his times, तिरुवाय्मोऌइ Piḷḷai and Kiḍāmbi Nāyanār. He thus became an expert in the Sanskrit scriptures as also the Tamil lore of Viśiṣṭādvaita.
He settled down at श्रीरङ्गम्. He was a householder at first. Later on, he embraced सṁन्यास (monastic life) receiving the monastic vows from Śaṭhagopa Jīyar.
He spent most of his time in giving religious discourses, writing books and helping in building temples or renovating old ones.
He toured widely, visiting all the important places connected with Śrīvaiṣṇa-vism. He was a prolific writer mostly in Tamil. Some of them are: commentaries on the important works of पिऌऌऐ लोकाचार्य (A.

-1327) such as Śrīvacana-bhūṣaṇa and Tattvatraya; Pramāṇat-tiraṭṭu; Yatirājaviṁśati; Upadeśaratna-mālai; Ārtiprabandha and Tiruvārādhana-krama.
He trained eight disciples—three were saṁnyāsins and the rest होउसे-holders—and appointed them as the pontiffs of the several Maṭhas (religious centres) such as Vānamāmalai मठ, Yatirāja मठ and others.
He emphasised the superiority of भक्ति (devotion) to God and service to the society in one’s personal life. Even members of the lower castes were his disciples.

Māṇikkavācagar
(9th or 10th cent. A. D.)
------------------------------------------
If the śivaśaraṇas (servants of Lord शिव) and the dāsas (servants of Lord विष्णु) spread the universal cult of भक्ति (devotion to God) in Karnataka, the Nāyanmārs and the आऌवार्स् (those immersed in the love of God) did the same in Tamil Nadu.
Among the sixty-three Nāyanmārs who were great devotees of शिव, Māṇikka-vācagar was an important person whose two great works Tiruvāsagam and Tirukkovai are popular even today.
Born of ब्राह्मण parents at Tiruvaḍuvūr (near मदुरै in Tamil Nadu) he became an adept in the know-ledge of the scriptures, especially the आगमस्. The Pāṇḍyan king, Arimarttanam by name, who had heard of his stupendous knowledge and uncanny wisdom as well as impeccable character, appointed him as his chief minister.
Once the king sent him on a mission to purchase imported Arab horses from Tirupirendūr. However, Mānikkavācagar met a great Śaiva saint (who was शिव himself), received spiritual instructions and utilised the money given by the king for purchasing the horses, to build a temple for शिव. The king jailed him for embezzlement of funds. But by the grace of शिव he was released. He resigned from his ministership and started roaming about as a minstrel of God. He is said to have defeated a band of Buddhist scholars in public debate at चिदम्बरम् (Chidambaram).
Of his two works Tiruvāsagam is autobiographical and reveals his spiritual struggles culminating in spiritual illumination.
The Tirukkovai depicts the longing of the सोउल् for शिव, but using erotic imagery.

maṇipravāḷa
(‘jewel and pearls’)
------------------------------------------
Tamiḷ and Malayāḷam are two languages considered of a Draviḍian origin and not derived from or related to Sanskrit. As Sanskrit became more and more popular, it also became a favourite of the scholars. There seems to have arisen a need to integrate it with Malayāḷam and Tamiḷ, and, produce a new style of composition. This came to be known as ‘maṇipravāḷam’ (maṇi = jewel like ruby or diamond; pravāḷa = pearl), Malayāḷam being the ‘maṇi’ and Sanskrit being the ‘pravāḷam’.
The origin of this style is attributed to the poet Tolan in the court of the king Kulaśekhara (circa 9th century A. D.).
Līlātilaka, a grammar of Malayāḷam, has systematised this style and has also evolved the necessary rules. It might have been composed around the middle of the 15th century.
In this style of writing, Malayāḷam words and Sanskrit words already present in the common language of the people have been fused into one.
The मणिप्रवाऌअ literature is generally divided into two styles, sandeśa and campū. Unnanīlīsandeśa composed probably during A.

is a typical work of the sandeśa group.
In the campū works, the poetry part is in Sanskrit metres. The prose part is in the style of Malayāḷam and Tamiḷ.
The Rāmāyaṇa-campū and the Bhāratacampū are two important works of this class.

Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is the smallest of the ten उपनिषद्स् and belongs to the Atharva-veda. It has only twelve verses, all in prose. But, it has been considered as basic to the principles of Vedānta, especially the Advaita Vedānta. An analysis of the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् viz., जाग्रत् (wakefulness), स्वप्न (dream) and सुषुप्ति (deep-sleep) and relating them to the three syllables a, u and m of प्रणव or ओङ्कार and establishing the तुरीय (literally ‘the fourth’) as the highest reality is the speciality of its teaching.
A brief account of the twelve verses may now be given here:
Verse 1: All this (the manifested world) is the syllable Om. Whatever exists in time—the past, the present and the future—as also whatever is beyond it, that too is Om.
Verse 2: All this is verily ब्रह्मन्. This आत्मन् (the individual सोउल्) is ब्रह्मन्. He has four aspects.
Verse 3: वैश्वानर, the आत्मन् associated with the waking state, is the first aspect. He cognises external objects. He has seven limbs like the sun, the air and the earth. He has nineteen mouths such as the sense-organs and the motor-organs. He experiences gross material objects.
Verse 4: तैजस, the second aspect is the आत्मन् associated with the dream state and cognises internal objects. He too has seven limbs and nineteen mouths and experiences the subtle objects.
Verse 5: The प्राज्ञ is the third aspect. He is the same आत्मन् associated with the deep-sleep state, where there are neither द्रेअम्स् nor desires. He is a solid mass of चोग्नितिओन्, full of bliss and enjoys bliss.
Verse 6: He is the lord of all, the knower of all and the inner controller. He is also the origin of this world.
Verse 7: The तुरीय is the fourth aspect of the आत्मन् as it were. He is different from the other three. He is indescribable since he is beyond the ken of all the senses. He is one without a second. He is the आत्मन् (Universal Self) who should be known or realised.
Verse 8: From the standpoint of the whole letter, the आत्मन् is Om. The three syllables of Om are a, u, and m.
Verse 9: वैश्वानर is the first syllable a. One who knows him thus will be able to attain all desires.
Verse 10: तैजस is the second syllable u. One who knows him thus increases his knowledge. In his family only knowers of ब्रह्मन् (= आत्मन्) are born.
Verse 11: प्राज्ञ is the third syllable, m. He who knows this, knows all and gets merged in all.
Verse 12: The Turīya—the ‘fourth’ as it were—is beyond all the three syllables. He it is into whom the world dissolves. He is one, beyond all dualities, and the very personification of auspiciousness. One who realises him, attains his own real self.
One of the four महावाक्यस् or ‘great sentences’, accepted by the Advaita Vedāntic tradition, viz., ayam ātmā brahma, occurs in the second verse.
Proving the existence of the आत्मन् as the pure conscious spirit, different from the body-मिन्द् complex, though existing in it or even identified with it, and, equating it with ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, the cause of and the spirit behind the universe is the main purpose of this Upaniṣad. The unique method used for this is the analysis of the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
There is a long expository treatise on this Upaniṣad called Kārikā or Māṇḍūkya-kārikā by गौडपाद (7th Century A. D.), teacher’s teacher of शङ्कर (A.

Māṇḍūkyakārikā
------------------------------------------
The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad belonging to the Atharvaveda is the shortest of the ten उपनिषद्स् considered as the major ones. It has the unique distinction of a detailed exposition by two stalwarts:—Śaṅkara (A.

-820) and his teacher’s teacher, गौडपाद (7th century A. D.).
Gauḍapāda (about whom we know next to nothing) (See GAUḌAPĀDA.) wrote a detailed commentary on this Upaniṣad, in the form of Kārikās (explanatory verses). His work is now well-known as the Māṇḍūkyakārikā. Āgamaśāstra is another name by which also it is known.
Though, apparently, this Kārikā is a commentary on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, in reality, it is much more than that. It looks as though गौडपाद has used this Upaniṣad as a means, to expound his own brand of Advaita Vedānta. Some people even go to the extent of not granting the status of an Upaniṣad to the Māṇḍūkyopa-niṣad and dub it as the च्रेअतिओन् of गौडपाद himself!
The Māṇḍūkyakārikā has a total of 215 verses divided into four prakaraṇas or sections. They are:
Āgama-prakaraṇa (29 verses)
Vaitathya-prakaraṇa (38 verses)
Advaita-prakaraṇa (48 verses)
Alātaśānti-prakaraṇa (100 verses)
The Āgamaprakaraṇa is a commentary on the entire Māṇḍūkyopaniṣad dividing it into four parts. The explanatory Kārikās are interspersed here and there as follows: Kārikās 1 to 9 after the sixth मन्त्र of the Upaniṣad; Kārikās 10 to 18 after the seventh मन्त्र; Kārikās 19 to 23 after the eleventh मन्त्र and the rest, Kārikās 24 to 29, after the last (the twelfth) मन्त्र.
The other three prakaraṇas are entirely independent expositions of Advaita Vedānta from various angles.
Śaṅkara has commented upon all the Kārikās also, apart from the Upaniṣad itself.
The Vaitathyaprakaraṇa deals with the Vaitathya or unreality of the world by analysing the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
The Advaitaprakaraṇa attempts to establish advaita (viz., that ब्रह्मन् is the one and only Reality) through yukti or लोगिच्.
The Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa, the longest of the four sections, refutes 35 schools of philosophy that existed during Gauḍa-pāda’s time, using the famous example of alāta or a lighted torch, which, when rotated, appears as a circle of fire, though no such circle really exists. In the same way, the dvaitaprapañca or the world of duality is only an appearance and not real.
Some of the more important concepts given by गौडपाद in this work may now be mentioned briefly.
Analysing the avasthātraya (See AVASTHĀTRAYA.) or the three states of consciousness—jāgrat (waking state), स्वप्न (dream state) and सुषुप्ति (deep-sleep state)—Gauḍapāda makes an important point: It is only in the waking state that the dream and the deep-sleep states are negated. However, from the standpoint of the तुरीय (the ‘fourth’ state) which is the eternal ‘waking state’ in the आत्मन्, even the so-called waking state also is filled with the darkness of इग्नोरन्चे! Compared to this, all the three states are actually the night of इग्नोरन्चे.
‘Ajāti’ or ‘non-birth’ is another concept which is peculiar to this work. (See AJĀTIVĀDA for details.) Since ब्रह्मन् alone is real and all other objects—whether it is this world or the jīvas (living beings)—are only appearances, there is no question of any ‘birth’ (jāti = birth) or च्रेअतिओन् of this world at all. Though the scriptures have described सृष्टि or च्रेअतिओन्, they have not declared it to be real!
However, following the beaten track of tradition and as a concession (out of compassion) to the ordinary sādhakas (spiritual aspirants) गौडपाद accepts praṇavopāsanā (meditation on आत्मन्/ ब्रह्मन्, with the help of प्रणव or ओङ्कार) and explains the procedure in detail.
Another special term used in this work is ‘asparśayoga’. It is the same as the experience of unalloyed bliss of the Self (Ātman/Brahman) wherein there is no sparśa or contact of the senses with their objects, but only with the Self (a = not; sparśa = contact; योग = union).
The Kārikā ends with a definition of मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् as just a rediscovery of one’s true nature as the आत्मन् (= ब्रह्मन्) and a brief description of the man of लिबेरतिओन्.
Ānandagiri (15th century A. D.) has written a gloss on the commentary of शङ्कर, elucidating further, wherever necessary.
See MĀṆḌŪKYA UPANIṢAD also.

maṇi
(‘gem’)
------------------------------------------
Wearing of precious gems to ward off evil or diseases and to gain health or a desired object seems to be an ancient practice. Even the Atharvaveda (1.29.1 to 6) mentions it.
Each of the gems recommended is supposed to have a perennial source of one specific ray which is not exhausted even after wearing it constantly for years.
These gems and the nine प्लनेत्स् are believed to have some mysterious connection. Hence, qualified and competent astrologers, by studying the होरोस्चोपे of a person suffering from a disease or upset by a calamity can prescribe the particular gem to be worn on the body by which the disease can be cured or calamity averted.
For instance, wearing of emerald can cure acidosis. Wearing of a red coral can avoid accidents.

maṇḍala
(‘a circular figure that embellishes’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘maṇḍala’ has been used in various senses in the Hindu scriptures and allied works depending upon the particular field of knowledge.
In the Ṛgveda it is the name of the ten books or sections into which it is divided, based on the subject content.
In the ritualistic field, it is a circular diagram containing squares and triangles, generally prepared with coloured powders. When consecrated it acts like a fence or border protecting the ritual from evil influences and forces. The names of some of the maṇḍalas are: Sarvatobhadra, Caturliṅgabhadra, Prāsādavāstumaṇḍala, Hariharamaṇḍala and so on.
A Hindu temple when viewed from above, represents a मण्डल.
In the works on political science (arthaśāstra or rājyaśāstra) मण्डल is a part of a king’s territory. A मण्डल is made up of four deśas, each deśa containing 100 villages. In some works, this definition has been reversed, making the मण्डल a subdivision of deśa.

-800)
------------------------------------------
According to the traditional biographies of शङ्कर (A.

) मण्डन मिश्र was a disciple of the well-known Mīmāṁsā scholar कुमारिल भट्ट (8th century A. D.). He was defeated by शङ्कर in disputation and became his disciple. After taking सṁन्यास, he was given the name Sureśvarācārya. His wife too became a saṁnyāsinī disciple of शङ्कर under the name उभयभारती.
However, this has been disputed by the modern scholars. Since मण्डन मिश्र was the author of a well-known work on Advaita Vedānta, the Brahmasiddhi, it is possible that he too was a Vedāntin, though holding views different from those of शङ्कर. According to these scholars, Sureśvarācārya was a different person whose original name was विश्वरूप.
The works attributed to Maṇḍana—all on the Mīmāṁsā—are: Vidhiviveka, Bhāvanāviveka, Vibhramaviveka and Mīmāṁsānukramaṇī.
Umbeka, a disciple of Kumārila, has written a commentary on Bhāvanāviveka.

maṇḍapa
------------------------------------------
In the works on Hindu architecture like the Mānasāra, this word (also spelt as maṇṭapa) is used in several senses. Generally it means a detached building, a pavilion or an open hall, with a roof supported on pillars, but without any wall-enclosure.
In temples, the small corridor in front of the गर्भगृह (santcum) is called शुकनासी or ardhamaṇḍapa or mukha-मण्डप. The general pavilion or hall is called मण्डप or nṛttamaṇḍapa which is used for congregational religious acts like singing, dancing or religious discourses.
The मण्डप should be built to the north or the east of the temple.

Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor उपनिषद्स् assigned to the Śukla Yajurveda. It was taught by आदित्य, the पुरुष (being) in the orb of the sun, to the sage याज्ञवल्क्य.
The Upaniṣad has five ब्राह्मणस् or chapters, thirteen khaṇḍas or subsections and eightynine mantras, both in prose and in poetry.
The first chapter starts with the story of the great sage याज्ञवल्क्य approaching आदित्य or the Sun-god (also called नारायण) for the knowledge of the आत्मन्. आदित्य starts his teaching by describing the aṣṭāṅgayoga (the योग comprising eight steps) leading to ज्ञान or knowledge of ब्रह्मन् (= आत्मन्). Though these eight steps appear to be the same as in the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) they are not. Here यम has four parts and नियम has nine. Items under these include forbearance of the vagaries of nature, steadiness of मिन्द्, devotion to the spiritual teacher, solitude, not desiring the fruits of action and self-control. आसन is that posture of meditation wherein the मिन्द् can easily flow towards ब्रह्मन्. Fixing the मिन्द् on the आत्मन् (the सोउल् inside oneself) as pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, after eliminating the mental waves of sense-objects is धारणा. Seeing the आत्मन् (pure चैतन्य or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्) in all living beings continuously is ध्यान. Forgetting oneself completely in this experience is समाधि.
This is followed by the enumeration of pañcadoṣas or five defects in an embodied being which are obstacles to मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्. They are काम (lust), krodha (anger), niśśvāsa (unsteadiness of breath), bhaya (fear) and निद्रा (sleep). They have to be conquered respectively by not making up one’s मिन्द्, forgiveness, प्राणायाम (breath-control), giving up the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of duality and thinking of the highest Truth.
Fixing the मिन्द् on the light in between the eyebrows along with some other details is described next.
The जीव (individual सोउल्) by following the disciplines described here, detaches himself from all the 24 principles of प्रकृति and realises that he himself is परमात्मन् (the Supreme Self) in essence.
Thus ends the first chapter.
The second chapter starts with the questions by याज्ञवल्क्य regarding some teachings in the last chapter which he has not grasped. In reply, the पुरुष in the orb of the sun (who is the teacher here) replies describing the आत्मन्/Brahman which is extremely brilliant and the cause of the five fundamental elements. This आत्मन्, which is also the final resting place of the universe after dissolution, can be attained only by ज्ञान (the path of knowledge leading to its experience). Here a few techniques of योग which are rather difficult to comprehend, are described.
Next comes a description of प्रणव (or ओङ्कार) as identified with ब्रह्मन् and the absence of the bondage of कर्म in him who has realised it.
The inner experience of a man of knowledge is next compared to a ritualistic worship. For instance, renunciation of all actions is आवाहन (inviting the deity to the place of worship). The continuous flow of the मिन्द् in the form of ब्रह्मन् is itself स्नान (bath) of the deity. The realisation, ‘I am He’ is itself नमस्कार (salutation) and so on.
Continuous meditation of ब्रह्मन् in this manner—if practised by the sādhaka or the votary—ultimately leads to its realisation.
There is an interesting पर here that shows the difference between सुषुप्ति (deep-sleep) and समाधि (perfect concentration resulting in the superconscious experience of the आत्मन्) since the मिन्द् is dissolved in both these experiences. In सुषुप्ति the मिन्द् is dissolved in तमस् (the basis of इग्नोरन्चे) and hence comes back with all its defects intact. In समाधि, तमस् is completely destroyed and the perception of the world (as a real object) is gone. Hence, even after coming out of समाधि, the realised सोउल् does not see the world as a real object but only as ब्रह्मन् and as identified with himself.
Then comes a description of five states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. They are: जाग्रत् (waking state), स्वप्न (dream state), सुषुप्ति (deep-sleep state), तुरीय (the fourth state) and turīyātīta (the state beyond even the तुरीय).
The जीव or the bound सोउल्, gradually progresses from the first to the last state through experiences got over several lives.
Now comes a delineation of the path that leads to the transcending of सṁसार (transmigration). This is the usual traditional path consisting of approaching the spiritual teacher, giving up all actions motivated by selfish desires, duly performing the prescribed duties, acquiring the four well-known sādhanās (viveka, वैराग्य and so on), meditating on ब्रह्मन् in the heart and realising the same.
The Upaniṣad declares here that सङ्कल्प (making up one’s मिन्द् to acquire and enjoy the objects of desire) is responsible for बन्ध (bondage) and giving it up, leads to मोक्ष (liberation).
One who gives up सङ्कल्प and sees the whole world as आत्मन्/Brahman is able to realise it in course of time and himself become that.
The third chapter which is short describes unmanībhāva and amanaskatva. When the various pratyayas or mental waves are looked upon as nothing but परमात्मन्, the Supreme Self, who is the final or original cause of all, including ब्रह्मा, विष्णु and रुद्र, and who is sporting in one’s heart or intellect, then, the effects of the इन्द्रियस् or the senses on the मिन्द् are destroyed. Then the मिन्द् will become absolutely steady like a lamp kept in a windless place. This itself is amanī-भाव (a state in which the मिन्द् does not behave like the original fickle मिन्द्).
This is also unmanībhāva, a state of transcending the मिन्द् and an experience of the bliss of ब्रह्मन्.
The fourth chapter is very short. It describes the vyomapañcaka or five kinds of ākāśas or space. They are: आकाश, parākāśa, mahākāśa, sūryākāśa and paramākāśa.
The ordinary physical space which is dark both inside and outside is the first, the आकाश. The parākāśa has the fire of deluge in it. The mahākāśa is that tattva or principle which is full of unlimited light. The sūryākāśa is brilliant like the sun. And, the paramākāśa is the all-pervading and indescribable light and is also full of bliss.
Here, the word आकाश in the latter, four terms, should be deemed to have been derived from the root-verb ‘kāś’ (‘to shine’). They are states of increasing enlightenment, of the knowledge of the आत्मन्/Brahman. The last is the final state.
The last chapter also is very short. After describing how the मिन्द् can be dissolved (manolaya) by detaching it from the world and directing it towards the Ādityapuruṣa (who is ब्रह्मन्), the text describes how a परमहṁस or an अवधूत, the perfected being, lives in the world. He is ever pure and detached. His purity and spiritual greatness are capable of liberating one hundred and one generations.
On the whole it can be said that the Upaniṣad, while not deviating from the usual (core) teachings of the major उपनिषद्स्, also gives a lot of information about the esoteric teachings of हठयोग and राजयोग.
